name: Palladian Construction Structural Echo Tap
description: Developed ostensibly as a structural integrity monitoring tool, the Structural Echo Tap transmits data by inducing precisely calibrated micro-vibrations into load-bearing concrete, rebar, and steel superstructures — the bones of GLMZ's perpetually under-construction cityscape. Receiving units detect and decode these vibrations using contact piezoelectric sensors pressed against the same structural members, reconstructing the signal from what appears to any passive observer as ordinary building settlement noise. The system was designed for Palladian Construction's own site supervisors to maintain covert communication channels in environments too electromagnetically hostile for conventional radio, but units have since proliferated well beyond authorized hands.

specifications.dimensions: Transmitter unit: 9cm x 5cm x 3cm flat plate with adhesive mounting surface; Receiver unit: 6cm x 4cm contact pad
specifications.range: Up to 400m through continuous structural material; degraded at material joins
specifications.detectability: Undetectable by RF spectrum analysis; requires contact seismic sensors to identify

tactical_use: The Tap is affixed to walls, floors, support columns, or pipe runs — any surface in continuous material contact with the target receive point. Because the signal travels through solid matter rather than air, it passes through Faraday cages, RF shielding, and signal-suppressed environments without attenuation. This makes it invaluable for communicating into or out of hardened secure facilities, holding cells, corporate black sites, and bunkers. Operators have developed a practice of mapping structural paths in advance — identifying which columns and beams connect which rooms — to plot reliable signal routes through complex buildings. Voice transmission is possible but degraded; short coded text bursts are the standard protocol.
cultural_context: Palladian Construction's near-monopoly on major civil construction in GLMZ means their rebar and poured concrete is in virtually every significant structure in the city. This ubiquity is not lost on those who use the Tap — there is dark humor in the fact that the city's physical skeleton has become a covert communications network. Among incarcerated fixers, political prisoners, and corporate detainees, the Tap is sometimes the only link to the outside world, passed in through bribed guards or concealed in personal effects. Palladian has never officially acknowledged the non-construction uses of the device, maintaining that all licensed units are for site management only.
known_users: Corporate extraction teams breaching shielded facilities
Resistance cells operating in signal-suppressed districts
story_hooks: A player receives an unexpected tap-signal through the floor of a safehouse — someone in the structure below is trying to make contact, but the message is partially corrupted and the sender's identity is unknown.

Palladian Construction quietly revokes the licenses of every Tap unit in a specific district just before a major demolition project begins — and someone suspects the demolition isn't about urban renewal.
A corporate prisoner has been tapping coded messages through her cell wall for six months. Someone has been answering. Neither party knows who the other is.

The players need to communicate with an asset inside a Faraday-shielded black site. Their only option is to find a structural contact point — which means going somewhere very dangerous to place the transmitter.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian flat plate device with a brushed steel face and a pronounced adhesive mounting surface. The transmitter resembles an industrial vibration sensor disguised as unremarkable construction hardware. Minimalist design with subtle accent lighting around its perimeter. The receiver is a smaller contact pad with a flexible piezoelectric element visible beneath transparent protective resin.
physical_description.dimensions: Transmitter 9cm × 5cm × 3cm (passport-sized flat plate); Receiver 6cm × 4cm (palm-sized contact pad)
physical_description.weight_description: Transmitter 180g (handheld, clip to tool belt or magnetic mount); Receiver 90g (pocketable, designed to press against structural members)
physical_description.primary_material: Transmitter: aerospace-grade aluminum chassis with reinforced mounting bracket; Receiver: polycarbonate housing with embedded piezoelectric transducer array
physical_description.finish: Transmitter: brushed gunmetal with industrial mil-spec texture; Receiver: matte charcoal with grip-textured contact surface
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray primary, with faint cyan accent lighting along the transmitter's edge; minimal branding in subdued white lettering
physical_description.interface_elements: Transmitter: single physical dial for frequency adjustment (8–40 Hz), three status LEDs (power/signal/encryption), micro-USB charge port recessed beneath rubber flap; Receiver: no interface—passive contact sensor with indicator gel on contact surface, single status LED buried under translucent resin dome
distinctive_features: Adhesive mounting surface on transmitter designed to adhere directly to concrete, steel, or rebar
Piezoelectric contact pad on receiver shows faint iridescent sheen under oblique light
Minimal industrial aesthetic—deliberately designed to blend with construction site equipment
Faint cyan pulse emanating from edge-mounted power indicator
Magnetic mounting bracket with quick-release mechanism on transmitter base
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: PALLADIAN CONSTRUCTION in subdued white sans-serif on transmitter face; small regulatory stamp (GLMZ-CERT-2218) on rear; no serial number visible on street-market units
physical_description.condition_typical: Transmitter shows dust and concrete particulate residue; faint scratches from mounting/remounting; receiver's contact gel slightly discolored from repeated use against various building materials
